Keep three numbers distinct: ~$4B of remediation-equivalent work is the engineering opportunity, what institutions would pay is the addressable market, what DocAble captures is a business question — MAGE needs only the first.

sections.heading_text: The Factory Is Also a Liability
sections.topic_sentence: Keeping the case honest requires the other ledger column, because everything this section has praised also has a failure mode.

points.text: A model kept naming a moved symbol and stayed authoritative-looking for days — accumulated structure fails in its own ways.
The liability list: models drift, controls conflict, evidence goes stale, gates encode obsolete assumptions, support machinery needs operating, and engineering capital depreciates.
The claim stays bounded: one longitudinal case, one primary engineer, one model ecosystem, no controlled comparison — the case establishes mechanism and sequence, not prevalence.

The transition: DocAble is one deliberately engineered response to abundant realization, so a factory has to be evaluated as a production system rather than by agent capability alone; the stronger question is whether independently developed factories exhibit the same pressures.

preamble_points.text: DocAble was built in roughly twenty weeks by one engineer directing a fleet of coding agents, at a volume beyond one person's reading.

New work did not originate in the agents or the factory's models. It came from engineering needs: goals, user feedback, production failures, standards obligations, advocacy guidance, and institutional use. The engineer decided which pressures became engineering work and made the consequential requirements, architecture, validation, and deployment decisions.

The existing engineering environment shaped how the work could be realized: architecture, tests, models, instructions, validators, deployment machinery, and accumulated controls carried earlier decisions. Agents implemented inside it, and the engineer's attention went to direction, evidence, admission, and changing the production system.

That division of work is the factory this section examines, and the chronology matters because none of it arrived fully formed: as realization accelerated, failures exposed missing representations, controls, and supervisory surfaces, and the production system changed in response.
The requirements were ordinary production-software requirements; the unusual condition was the implementation capacity available to one engineer.

sections.topic_sentence: Five of the seven accounts describe a system an organization built for its own work, and each enters from a different problem.

points.text: Five accounts describe systems an organization built for its own work, each entering from a different problem; four delegate software realization to agents from the existing environment, while Zenseact's agents do knowledge work around its factory rather than realization inside it.

sections.topic_sentence: Uber reports a factory operating at the largest scale in this corpus: more than 70 percent of pull requests attributed to local or cloud agents, more than 3,600 engineer-created agent skills executing over 30,000 times per day, and managed agents performing code review, CI repair, end-to-end changes, alert triage, debugging, and maintenance.[cite: medisetty2026factory] The headline figure needs its measurement caveat attached: no source defines "attributed to," and figures published earlier the same year under narrower definitions were far lower — 11 percent of pull requests *opened* by agents as of March.[cite: orosz2026uber] The scale is real; its denominator is not public.

points.text: Uber reports the corpus's largest realization share — over 70 percent of PRs attributed to agents, 3,600 skills, 30,000 executions daily — but the attribution is undefined, and earlier same-year figures under narrower definitions were far lower; work increasingly originates from the factory's own operational signals.

The fabricator receives a governed, pre-compiled environment and produces its own evidence in an inner loop attached to the PR — a table the producing agent assembles about its own work, with no independent re-derivation stated — and admission stays human: "we still have humans approving the code," with automatic approval a named destination whose criterion is unpublished and review capacity the measured constraint.

Supervision is structured by measurement, asymmetrically: benchmarks from real workloads and outcome-denominated costs are published in detail, while the named quality signals are tracked and never published; the reasoning surface is a knowledge graph, not a model of the software's behavior — and Uber's own closing note moves the bottleneck to human judgment.

sections.topic_sentence: Cloudflare's factory attaches to its engineering organization at review rather than at origination: engineers still open the merge requests and write the specs, and the agentic apparatus evaluates them.

points.text: Cloudflare's agentic apparatus attaches at review: a purpose-built agent extracts the RFC corpus into structured statements with stable identities, applied at four or five stations across the lifecycle — with the linter-versus-review line drawn by mechanical verifiability per language, motivated by latency rather than a taxonomy.

Admission is machine-held in the ordinary case — a coordinator agent approves, revokes, or blocks with no human in the path — bounded by human-authored policy, an approval-biased rubric, and a logged break-glass override used on 0.6 percent of merge requests.

Failures convert into environmental structure along four documented paths — named rules from named outages, Snapstone enrolment, representation revision, a new linter station — but no loop is closed by measurement, and Cloudflare itself calls the agent-evaluation loop unfinished.

sections.topic_sentence: Spotify's production line predates its agent by years.

points.text: Spotify's fleet line — targeting from BigQuery and the Backstage software catalog, Fleetshift execution, automerge, post-merge monitoring — predates the agent by years; the agent replaced the deterministic transform at one station, everything else "remains exactly the same," and it took over the residual the prior technique could not reach.

The agent's freedom is set environmentally — a verify tool, restricted git, an allowlisted shell, with code search deliberately withheld — a PR may not exist until verification passes, and the LLM judge added against scope creep was later removed as models improved: a control retired, not just installed.

Deterministic fleet changes automerge by default — 2.5 million maintenance PRs, most with no human in the loop — while agent-authored PRs wait for human review, the named bottleneck; incident retrospectives ask whether AI-authored code contributed, and the published constraint is verification capacity.

sections.topic_sentence: At Shopify, work originates in a conversation held in the open.

points.text: Work originates in open Slack conversations with River — no direct messages by design — with one in eight merged PRs coauthored as of May 2026, channels roughly doubling by September while the people count stayed flat, and a founder-stated half-of-PRs origination share that is a different measure.

The session corpus is mined into skills and instruction files by people, with the effect measured and the counterfactual controlled — merge rate 36 to 77 percent in two months without retraining or switching models; "multiplayer by construction" is Shopify's advice to readers, not its self-description, and no automated extraction is established.

A September security-workflow account specifies the admission machinery — draft-only output, human merge authority, a freshness-gated merge queue, post-merge verification — and the rule that guarantees belong in code, not prompts; the stated grounding for the human gate is responsibility rather than evidence adequacy, reported only at second hand; the record does not say what governs the rest of River's output.

sections.topic_sentence: Zenseact, a driver-assistance software company, belongs in this section with a scoping sentence attached: its agents do not produce software.

points.text: Zenseact's ZAP agents query Gerrit, Zuul, JIRA, and SAP as data sources and produce answers, not changes — not an agentic software factory under this chapter's definitions — and the case stays for the federation move: platform team owns a runtime with no business logic, a domain agent is a directory with two text files.

ZAP's admission unit is the tool call, its context routing is deterministic and measured, and its distinctive loop types routing failures and repairs the representation — the skill file — rather than the model.

sections.topic_sentence: GitLab belongs in the other column because the capability its account describes is generalized and sold, to be attached to somebody else's repositories, policies, and engineering knowledge.

points.text: GitLab belongs in the factory-in-a-box column because it generalizes and sells the production capability — and its own handbook now documents the internal practice too: failing-test-first doctrine, CI as the gate, a test-count guard, and a dated 95-percent-agent-generated service built atop four weeks of harness construction.

A factory in a box introduces a boundary an internal factory does not have: the vendor supplies fabricator, orchestration, context machinery, evidence, and generic controls, and the engineering problem is integration, not installation — at both ends of the production line.

Upstream, intent enters GitLab's machinery as files the customer authors at fixed repository paths, under the vendor's stated thesis that anything the agent cannot access in context effectively does not exist; the vendor-recovered context graph supplies relationships, not the intent the customer never wrote down.

Downstream, admission authority stays human by construction — "The flow never sets the Approve state, even when it finds no issues" — with agent privileges intersected with the triggering human's, tool policy tightenable but never loosenable, and audit machinery that records the human decision without moving it.

The public record is specific about infrastructure and silent about the knowledge-authoring cost — no case study of a customer writing those files, no measure of output against their quality — and the layer that produced GitLab's own 95-percent service is precisely the layer only the customer can author.
The externalization question follows directly from the two-ended boundary and is worth stating plainly.

The question restates the Modeling problem in commercial terms, and the factory chapter already named the tradeoff behind it: a purchased factory that works only when the buyer describes the software almost completely has recreated the arrangement the earlier software factories died of.

sections.topic_sentence: Siemens sits at the end of the second axis the software-first accounts do not reach.

points.text: Model-first production inverts where intent enters: explicit engineering models, not the repository and its tests, carry the system's semantics, and the software is generated downstream of them.

The load-bearing Siemens evidence is Eigen — control code generated from a TIA Portal engineering model, iterating until pre-defined performance benchmarks are met, a tolerance in this chapter's exact sense — and the 2024 Agent Studio research on SysML v2 with simulation as validator: a model supplies goal and context, a deterministic engine supplies the verdict.

The broader agentic-engineering architecture Siemens publishes is an explicit research vision about simulation, not software realization; no source establishes a model-implementation conformance gate, and Eigen's public record names no human approval step at all — while the one account of Siemens changing its own software keeps a human in the loop at every step and grounds that gate in a compliance obligation.

The sharp difference from the old model-driven dream is that today's fabricator is cheap and capable at once, so a model-first factory need not determine every realization decision — only the consequential ones.

Model-first is a position on one axis rather than a maturity level, and the axis is independent of the first — Siemens itself partially fills the combined cell, selling model-first factories in a box for the narrow software of control logic and chip design, while no observed case sells one for general-purpose software.

sections.heading_text: What the Factories Share, and Where They Differ
sections.topic_sentence: Across the seven accounts, four moves recur strongly enough to form a shared baseline.

points.text: Four moves recur across all seven: knowledge externalized, action bounded, generation separated from evidence, consequential decisions kept human — on three different stated groundings, evidence adequacy, responsibility, and compliance — plus Uber's fifth, the environment continuously measured.

The factories differ in where admission sits, how much knowledge they route into each task, whether failure-to-structure conversion is measured (the mechanism is documented nearly everywhere; aggregate yield once, class-recurrence nowhere), and — most sharply — how explicitly they model the governed system; no ordering follows.

The observed modeling frontier: the software-first accounts publicly show knowledge and governance representations; Siemens crosses into machine-checkable system models from a model-first tradition; DocAble additionally checks selected model-implementation relations and gives them consequences.

At organizational scale the recurring structure is leverage: one policy shapes thousands of changes, one representation guides a fleet, one learned constraint protects every later task — the organizational face of engineering capital.

preamble_points.text: DocAble is one system built by one engineer for one problem; the natural question is how engineers in other organizations, under different constraints, approach the same problem.

Seven public accounts are reconstructed; they differ in what they represent, how they direct and constrain agents, what evidence they require, where they keep human judgment — and in whether the factory is built for their own software or for somebody else's.

The commercial systems differ in architecture and organizational setting but share an emphasis on organizing agentic production — supplying context, structuring work, controlling tool access, arranging human review, and determining what may proceed — which matches process-oriented accounts of agentic software engineering.
The factories differ along two dimensions: who supplies the production system, and how engineering intent enters production.

The first distinction is between an internal factory, built and operated by an organization to change its own software, and a factory in a box, a generalized production system supplied to other organizations.

The second distinction concerns how engineering intent enters the factory: existing-environment-first factories give agents repositories, tests, pipelines and organizational context to recover what they need, while a model-first factory places explicit engineering models upstream of realization.
The two distinctions are independent: either factory form can be existing-environment-first or model-first, and the seven public accounts occupy only part of that design space.
The entry-points figure locates where each organization starts and where it invests; it shows emphasis, not maturity.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble's emphasis on tolerance was partly a consequence of the problem that produced it.

points.text: DocAble's emphasis on tolerance followed from its circumstances: accessibility supplied external legal obligations, and one engineer with no spare humans to inspect agent output had little process to design and every reason to encode requirements precisely.

Commercial agents work inside large engineering organizations where work moves among people, authority must be bounded, and changes enter systems many people maintain, so those factories emphasize process design; the difference is where the visible machinery is concentrated.

Tests, static checks, simulators, benchmarks, and policy predicates are genuine tolerance machinery, but much of the intent in the public accounts stays in natural language, which does not itself provide a machine-checkable boundary around acceptable realizations.

DocAble's tolerance is distinctive: MAGE represents the consequential property explicitly and uses Alignment to maintain correspondence with the realized system, so the tolerance is the represented obligation rather than any particular checking technique, which permits tighter tolerances than instructions or isolated checks alone.

Process design encodes assumptions about how production must proceed, which a better fabricator can change; tolerances describe properties the product must preserve, which a better fabricator does not change.

MAGE concentrates on the tolerance side and does not prescribe a general process, so the distinction is not between factories that have tolerances and factories that do not, but between ways of representing them, establishing them, and making them consequential.

sections.topic_sentence: In both aspects of factory engineering, human engineers use their judgment to decide what the production system should carry.

points.text: Both problems require human judgment — about decomposition, information, authority, review, and admission on one side, and about which properties are consequential and what evidence establishes them on the other — exercised once so it shapes subsequent production.

Organizations delegate judgment to people partly through incentives and accountability, and agents sit outside every one of those loops, so the human engineer decides which decisions may remain with the agent and which need stronger control through the production system.

A tolerance preserves engineering control without specifying the realization: the engineer names the consequential property and the evidence required for it, and the agent keeps the remaining degrees of freedom.

sections.heading_text: Factories Inside and Outside the Organization
sections.topic_sentence: The cases also differ in who supplies the factory.

points.text: The cases differ in who supplies the factory: some are internal production systems whose owners engineer the machinery their agents work through, while others move toward a reusable factory in a box supplied to organizations the provider does not own.

Every software factory must join productive capability to organization-specific engineering intent; an internal factory builds that connection directly, and a factory in a box must solve the same problem across an organizational boundary.

A provider can supply agents, orchestration, context, execution, permissions, evidence infrastructure, and generic controls, but cannot know which properties of a customer's software are consequential, so the customer's engineering knowledge must enter generic production machinery.

How a factory in a box exposes machinery for process design, for product tolerances, or for both remains an open design space; the narrower point is that productive capacity and engineering control need not come from the same place.

preamble_points.text: The factories differ in scale, organization, and purpose, and they place engineering structure in different parts of production: the commercial systems arrange how production proceeds, while much of DocAble's explicit structure represents properties of the software being produced.

Process design determines how production proceeds and tolerance determines what variation in the product is acceptable; both are problems of factory engineering, and the cases show how differently a factory can distribute its effort between them.

sections.topic_sentence: [ref:mage-dynamic-model] puts the theory on one diagram.

points.text: Agentic capacity and the governed environment jointly shape realized performance: throughput, defect escape, attention consumed.
Mismatch shows as churn, escaped defects, and friction; symptoms signal a problem but not which one.
The feedback loop: prior knowledge seeds the environment; work exposes gaps; diagnosis improves it; ambition repeats.

The feedback structure has a cybernetic heritage; Conant and Ashby's good regulator theorem connects regulation to representation — the regulated object changed, but the model-regulation link remains.
The environment represents consequential properties, observes work, and changes when its representations or controls prove inadequate.
Durable structure has two routes: before failure from known obligations, after experience from use (governance conversion).
Adaptation reaches the shared environment only with structural diagnosis and a path with authority to change it.

sections.topic_sentence: The dynamic model suggests a broader question: where can engineering intervene to improve agentic work?

points.text: Engineering can intervene at model, environment, process, representation, or evidence.
One school locates leverage in the engineering process around agents.
MAGE weights the engineered environment and its representations most heavily.
These leverage sources are complementary, differing in emphasis and mechanism.

sections.topic_sentence: More machinery does not mean a better environment.

points.text: More machinery is not a better environment; what counts is fit to the work, not how much machinery exists.
An effective environment needs useful representations, adequate coverage, coherence, and economy.
The four properties jointly determine how much consequential work still rests on fallible per-instance inference.
Coverage need not mechanize every obligation; a strong environment names where judgment belongs and where paying repeatedly is wasteful.
These are not maturity stages; improve whichever part of the environment is limiting the work.

sections.topic_sentence: A theory of agentic engineering should distinguish activity from progress.

points.text: The theory distinguishes activity from progress via three outcomes: durable throughput, defect escape, human-attention burden.
Durable throughput survives rework; defect escape reaches later stages; attention burden is judgment consumed per unit.
Human attention is not an implementation detail of governance; it is one of the scarce resources the engineered environment is intended to conserve.
Easy-to-count quantities (commits, lines, control files, support ratio) measure activity or investment, not outcome.

sections.topic_sentence: Three predictions form the core of the theory.

points.text: Three core predictions concern three ways an engineered environment can help.
Environment fit, representation leverage, and engineering capital are related but distinct effects.
Environment fit moderates the effect of velocity: added capacity yields throughput when the environment fits and churn when it does not; raw velocity may rise either way.
A trustworthy task-relevant model lowers the cost of acceptable realization by reducing reconstruction; it fails if upkeep outweighs reach.
Durable structure lets later work inherit judgment, but the return lasts only while the asset stays fit.
Each core proposition can fail; they are testable propositions, not guarantees.

sections.topic_sentence: Why should representation create leverage in the first place?

points.text: Answering an engineering question first requires reconstructing enough of the system to know what it means.

Larger context and retrieval postpone the horizon; DocAble met the limit literally — roughly 590,000 tokens of reasoning representation against a 272,000-token context made windowing and whole-document compression the next representation problem.
The general move: a useful model changes the problem by presenting the consequential structure directly — the basis for the reasoning-horizon proposition.
A model shortens the reasoning path, not merely each step: reasoning already performed is preserved in the environment.
Like a map, a model's value is preserving the relationships a class of questions needs while suppressing detail.
Agents do not create the scale problem; they change its economics and frequency, raising the return on representations.
Representations put consequential structure into a form the reasoner can use directly, not merely store facts.
Leverage can originate bottom-up: implementation signals can recover a latent model the system already embodies.
Representation innovation: a reasoner may propose a decomposition or state space under which a question becomes tractable.
Representations can be human-designed, machine-induced, or machine-innovated, each extending the effective reasoning horizon.
Discovery does not confer trust: a machine-proposed representation still must earn trust in the relationship it claims.
Representation engineering is bidirectional: humans extend machine reasoning and machines may recover or invent abstractions.

sections.topic_sentence: Representation leverage explains how structure can make one episode of reasoning easier.

points.text: Repeatedly reconstructing the same fact or judgment pays for the same reasoning; some judgments can instead be preserved.
Engineering capital: prior engineering work leaves behind productive capacity that future work can inherit.

Capital, not memory: an asset becomes capital when it changes future cost or risk, and it can depreciate — while the investment threshold itself moves as agentic capacity lowers construction and maintenance costs.
Capital transfers judgment beyond its originator: a later reasoner benefits without reconstructing the reasoning.
The transfer is partial: capital carries only what it represents, so change requires expert judgment again.
Debt makes change costly, capital makes it productive; neither is permanent, so governance includes retirement.
Debt has three interacting forms — technical, cognitive, intent — which GenAI can accelerate together.
A GEE counters technical and intent debt with durable structure and preserves the understanding needed for cognitive debt.
Capital gives knowledge, intent, and judgment a durable home; governance decides which assets stay trustworthy.

sections.heading_text: Modeling and Alignment Are Distinct—and Compound
sections.topic_sentence: The previous propositions explain why durable structure can help, but they combine two effects that MAGE keeps separate.

points.text: Durable structure combines two separable effects: helping the reasoner answer, and controlling whether a bad answer gains consequence.
Modeling changes the representation reasoned over; Alignment enforces selected obligations; either can help without the other.
A model can help without enforcing; a mechanism can govern even when the producer never sees the rule.
Two distinct problems: help the agent produce acceptable work, and ensure the forbidden result cannot enter regardless.

sections.topic_sentence: We can make the distinction precise by considering cost and failure separately.

points.text: One role of Modeling: raise per-attempt success or lower per-attempt cost, so acceptable realization is cheaper to find.
The ratio matters more than either term: a representation that raises attempt cost can still lower expected realization cost when its increase in p_R is large enough.

Cheap articulation can be expensive in expectation; a stronger reasoner raises p_R at inference cost, a better representation changes the problem — so Modeling trades representational investment against realization cost and reasoning capability.

Representation precedes model selection: ask what representation makes the problem available for reasoning before asking which reasoner should solve it — in DocAble, a practical cost rule: improve the representation before buying more inference.

The probabilities belong to a production system: the factory of Chapter 5, redrawn with each step of the realization path carrying the probability that it succeeds and the encoded property also supplying the tolerance the result is evaluated against.
The distinction matters because improving the fabricator and improving the tolerance act differently on this system.

An analytical (not independence-claiming) factorization of p_R into encode, interpret, and realize stages exposes the asymmetry: a stronger reasoner improves interpretation and realization but cannot recover intent that was never encoded.

The two factory techniques act on different factors: process design raises the interpretation and realization terms by improving the conditions around the fabricator, while tolerance engineering acts on encoding and lets acceptance rest on something other than the fabricator having got it right.

The interpretation factor also depends on how much inference the representation asks the agent to supply, and that burden varies: where the intended solution follows well-represented patterns, a sparse specification can still interpret well.

Other things equal, novelty is one factor that reduces the usefulness of the agent's prior as a substitute for explicit representation: specification supplies explicit engineering intent where inference from prior patterns is least dependable.

Familiarity solves the production problem but does not establish the property: unless the consequential property is represented, the environment cannot distinguish following the intended pattern from producing something that looks right.

Raising the interpretation factor does not retire explicit models or Alignment: learned priors reduce how much must be specified for realization without supplying an assurance surface for consequential properties.

The same limit applies to process design: it improves how an agent interprets natural-language intent, but an obligation left in natural language may require another act of probabilistic interpretation to establish that the result satisfies it, so tolerance supplies an independently evaluable boundary instead.
The interpretation factor is conditional not only on encoding quality and agent capability but also on the familiarity of the intended interpretation relative to what the agent already knows.

Encoding failure belongs largely to the human/factory interface: failing to articulate a consequential distinction and failing to recover it are different failures, and the entitlement case shows a representation that could not express the intent at all.
The asymmetry: capability can compensate for difficult interpretation but not for missing intent, so Modeling helps both before implementation begins — and can sometimes remove the judgment entirely.

In the limit of a perfect reasoner — interpretation and realization approaching certainty — p_R remains bounded by the encoding factor, so capability purchases cannot discharge an obligation the organization never externalized.

Perfect fabrication does not eliminate the engineering problem upstream of fabrication — it exposes it: a stronger reasoner can reconstruct much, but cannot reliably recover consequential knowledge that never entered the factory.

Read in factory terms the bound limits process design — it cannot make an incorrectly encoded obligation correct — and tolerance exposes a different limit: with a property represented explicitly and independently evaluated, better fabrication drives interpretation and realization error down while the remaining error approaches the probability that the engineering representation itself is wrong.

The bound does not argue for complete specification — that would recreate the earlier software factories' economics; the new possibility is realization freedom with the smaller set of consequential decisions explicitly preserved.

With carrying cost explicit, a representation can be economically preferable even when it is more expensive to construct and each realization through it is more expensive — it need only improve satisfactory realization enough, especially over repeated use.

Commodity intelligence changes both sides of the investment: greater implementation capacity can justify richer engineering structure while reducing the cost of carrying it, so the carrying term is not a fixed parameter of the environment.

Compensating for weak explicit representation by buying frontier reasoning is a prediction of the theory, not an objection: a factory that keeps consequential properties inside natural-language inference purchases reliability again on every change, while explicit tolerance converts some of that recurring inference into durable structure whose cost sits in the carrying term.

Across n realizations the fixed representation cost amortizes and the judgment embodied in the representation is reused — the factories accumulating shared policy, models, and permissions at scale are amortizing judgment, not adding process.

The factories differ in where they carry engineering knowledge; the decomposition explains why those arrangements can coexist, and the relevant question is what probability and cost of satisfactory realization an arrangement produces and what knowledge survives for the next task.
A sound admission gate makes covered failure impossible to admit regardless of how the producer reasoned.
Alignment makes consequence independent of whether the producing reasoner got the covered judgment right.
Assurance without useful representation is expensive: rejected candidates regenerate, so realization cost climbs.
The same admission guarantee over two reasoning surfaces produces substantially different realization costs.
Hiding the model does not weaken a perfect gate; it only raises the cost of reaching an acceptable candidate.
Alignment protects the boundary; Modeling reduces how often work collides with it.

Modeling can act at several stages before admission — stating intent, recovering it, easing realization — while Alignment acts afterward or alongside realization by determining whether covered failures can acquire consequence.
Their primary contributions are separable — Modeling and Alignment are different levers.

sections.topic_sentence: The analysis so far uses a simplification to isolate repeated probabilistic exposure: if consequential judgments have some probability of success and successive exposures are treated as independent, their joint probability of success falls as the number of exposures grows.

points.text: The simple models deliberately isolated repeated probabilistic exposure under fixed conditions.
Software engineering needs a different model: each realization becomes structure inherited by the next.

The factorization describes one realization whether it creates a system or changes one; change differs because it inherits architecture, representations, conventions, obligations, tests, and capital from earlier work.
Independence omits the inherited environment; success at each step depends on the environment carried into it.

Creation is realization from an initial environment, change is realization given an inherited one, and each realization determines the environment later work inherits — so the factory produces a sequence of changes, not independent realizations.
The coupling creates path dependence: poor structure makes good realization harder, and decay can become self-reinforcing.
The reverse trajectory: a realization that improves capital carries useful structure forward for later work.
The independent model isolates repeated exposure; the dynamic model preserves the coupling between realizations and environments.

sections.topic_sentence: The two principles interact in a second way.

points.text: Modeling can turn a semantic obligation into a checkable one by changing the object over which it is decided.
Two kinds of hard question look alike in code: intrinsically judgmental, or buried in the wrong representation.

The determinization frontier separates judgment supplied per instance from judgment the environment can carry repeatably — in factory terms, an economic boundary between judgments still bought probabilistically through the production process and properties made durable as tolerances.
DocAble's default: everything that could be deterministic was; commodity intelligence only where the problem requires semantic judgment.
Moving the frontier reduces the probabilistic surface without making the agent deterministic or removing realization freedom.
The frontier moves incrementally: from prose to invariant to bounded-model checking to temporal specification.
Moving the frontier governs obligations, not the acceptable ways to satisfy them, which remain degrees of freedom.
At the limit a complete realization model makes realization a transformation, connecting MAGE to model-based engineering.

sections.topic_sentence: We can now put the pieces back together.

points.text: The objective is an economical division of labor among reasoner, environment, and remaining human judgment.
An engineer jointly chooses a representation and an Alignment strategy, trading carrying cost against realization and failure cost.

Schematically: Modeling changes realization cost, Alignment changes failure consequence, and both impose carrying cost — and the minimization prices the factory's standing choice between buying inference quality repeatedly and making a property durable as a tolerance.

sections.topic_sentence: The expression above prices one realization.

points.text: A factory is an investment in productive capacity, so its economics cannot be evaluated from construction cost alone.

Software preserves the investment structure but changes what is produced: the factory does not manufacture each copy consumed, and its recurring output is the continued transformation of a maintained software system.
The cost model separates factory construction from continued production: startup cost, a stream of change costs, carrying cost, and expected failure loss.

The marginal question matters most: a successful factory may be expensive to construct and economical to use, because the productive capacity makes the stream of subsequent changes cheaper, faster, safer, or possible at all.

sections.topic_sentence: Software adds a distinction manufacturing does not have, and it should be stated explicitly: there are two margins here, not one.

points.text: Software has two distinct margins, a major difference from manufacturing: the production margin (the next acceptable change) and the replication margin (serving that change's benefit to the next user).

sections.topic_sentence: Carrying cost also divides, and the division is where the physical analogy breaks most instructively.

points.text: Carrying cost splits into operational carry and capital maintenance: a software factory can be cheap to leave physically idle while its engineering capital continues to depreciate.

sections.topic_sentence: Against these costs stands what the stream of changes is worth, and that side of the comparison is deliberately left abstract, because it cannot be specified universally.

points.text: What the stream of changes is worth cannot be specified universally: each factory's outcome quantities are themselves models of value chosen for a particular engineering or organizational decision.
The economic chain runs factory → software capability → use → value, and MAGE primarily concerns the first arrow; the organization's business model determines how capability becomes value.

sections.heading_text: Correctness Is Not the Factory's Objective
sections.topic_sentence: Correctness, however, is still not the factory's final objective.

points.text: The probability model explains the terms of the lifecycle factory economics: higher p_R raises durable throughput and lowers the cost of a change; Alignment exchanges validation cost for reduced escape risk; models preserve reasoning as engineering capital.
Correctness alone does not establish value: a factory can reliably and efficiently produce software that nobody needs.

The economic interpretation of Modeling and Alignment: valuable where the cost of externalizing, preserving, and enforcing consequential knowledge is lower than the expected cost of repeatedly reconstructing it, incorrectly realizing it, or allowing its violation to escape.

Commodity intelligence moves the boundary: the engineering problem does not disappear as fabrication approaches perfection — it moves toward deciding what must be preserved, inferred, established before admission, and what the capability is worth.
Chapter 5 supplied depth and variation, not population effect sizes; the theory is the proposed explanation of it.

preamble_points.text: This section proposes one explanation for both evidence-chapter views: the deep case and the broad variation.
The theory is directional, not numerical: it names the main parts, how they interact, and the relationships that should hold under stated conditions.
The central claim: agentic capacity acts through the engineered environment, which turns it into progress or churn.
Two limitations (finite horizon, residual risk) drew two responses (representation, enforcement) and a broader Chapter 5 set of responses.

Chapter 5 identified the economic tradeoff in where engineering judgment is carried; this chapter makes it precise, beginning with deliberately narrow models of probability and cost, after which the dynamic model widens the unit to capacity, environment, adaptation, and payoff.

sections.topic_sentence: Brownfield software raises the first problem immediately: can a useful engineering model be recovered from a system that was never built around one?

points.text: Brownfield's first problem: a recovered model must state what the system should do, not canonize what it does.
The second problem is maintaining the specific correspondence each model claims, cheaply enough to expose divergence early.
The third problem is quality: a synchronized model can still fail to capture the obligations decisions run through.
H1: a trustworthy task-relevant model reduces reasoning cost per acceptable realization, more so as required state grows.
H2: stale or mismatched models lose the H1 benefit, so correspondence and coverage should predict later churn or escape.
H3: for some obligations, an explicit representation makes a repeatable predicate feasible where implementation needs semantic reconstruction.
H4: commodity intelligence can induce latent structure and propose new representations that extend the reasoning horizon when validated.

sections.topic_sentence: Governance conversion remains primarily an act of judgment.

points.text: Governance conversion is primarily judgment; the frontier is deciding which investment is warranted and its cheapest adequate form.
A repository-access example: representing permitted paths and checking them is capital only if it retires the failure class cheaply.
Adaptive governance must also subtract: reduce consequential gaps without merely multiplying mechanisms.
What matters is whether a working path connects diagnosis to change in the shared environment.
H5: repeatable independent mechanisms reduce defect escape at matched throughput, excluding covered failure regardless of producer reliability.
H6: structural interventions reduce recurrence of a failure class net of carrying cost, non-monotonically once controls over-accumulate.
H7: lessons reach later work faster and survive personnel turnover better when diagnosis connects to shared machine-actionable structure.

sections.topic_sentence: The economic predictions are the least settled of the three families.

points.text: The economic predictions are least settled: estimating return needs a counterfactual amid moving capability and prices.
Durable structure can make later work cheaper or safer, but its return may not divide cleanly among individual artifacts.
The quantities that matter are returns and carrying costs, and how they change as the asset depreciates.
Effective capability may belong partly to the environment: a weaker model over a rich environment can outperform a stronger one.
Measure capital by fixing the agent and task, varying the environment, and measuring the capability it contributes.
H8: added capacity yields throughput and lower attention where the environment fits, and churn where it fits poorly.
Outer-loop corollary: stronger environments let intelligence assume more of the realization loop without proportionate attention growth.

H9: durable structures return when cost reductions exceed construction and carrying costs; returns decline as fit is lost and reconciling beats accumulating; rising agentic capacity lowers construction and maintenance costs, moving the investment threshold.

preamble_points.text: If the theory is right, certain consequences should follow wherever MAGE applies; they are derived, not findings.
The predictions fall into three families: trustworthy representations, adaptive governance, and engineering economics.

sections.topic_sentence: Whether MAGE applies to a given engineering surface comes down to three questions:

points.text: Whether MAGE applies comes down to three questions: return, adequate governability, and authority to act.
Return comes usually from recurrence but also from consequence: does avoided future cost justify construction and carrying cost?
Governability is how well an obligation can be made explicit, evidenced, and evaluated; deterministic checking is its strongest region, not its definition.
The residual probabilistic surface is not necessarily debt; some judgment belongs there, so do not minimize it blindly.
Authority is the organizational condition: a functioning path must connect diagnosis to the shared environment, or fixes stay local.
These scope conditions are theoretical, informed by the evidence chapter, not population estimates.

sections.heading_text: The Expanding Frontier of Explicit Engineering
sections.topic_sentence: MAGE's scope is not fixed because explicit engineering is becoming cheaper and, in some cases, more feasible.

points.text: MAGE's scope is not fixed: two interacting-but-independent questions govern it — economic return and feasible governability.
Consequence does not imply governability: some consequential obligations remain substantially qualitative however carefully evaluated.
Chapter 4 showed the boundary both ways: a broad judgment can stay probabilistic while narrower obligations within it become enforceable, and the residency model became a quantitative invariant.
Full formalization is an important region of the design space, not the endpoint of a ladder.
Where governability is limited, added consequence can justify more investment without making complete formalization feasible.
Value of explicit engineering and feasible governability are two dimensions; high value need not imply high governability.
Commodity intelligence first lowers the cost of explicit structure, so assets repay at lower recurrence or consequence.
Commodity intelligence can also increase governability, turning expert judgment into narrower evaluable or decidable properties.
These movements need not end in formalization; explicit engineering still pays when it makes judgment better informed and repeatable.
MAGE concerns the whole design space, not progress toward ever greater formalization; the objective is an economical division of work.
MAGE applies across scales — engineer, team, product, organization — with explicit correspondence keeping the scales distinct yet connected.
Scale and assurance strength are separate choices; organization-wide adoption does not imply maximal formalization.

sections.heading_text: The frontier is not a destination
sections.topic_sentence: Neither change should be mistaken for a destination for software engineering as a whole.

points.text: The frontier is not a destination: many questions stay open because the system's shape is still being discovered, so evolution remains an outer loop.
The failure mode is premature closure: a small probabilistic surface can mean the environment determinized the wrong problem.
Engineering capital can move the frontier within a system, enlarging the region of work later delegable to search.
MAGE predicts a moving economic boundary, not convergence toward complete specification; where it moves is empirical.
Scope should be judged surface by surface — recurrence, consequence, representability, carrying cost — not assigned to a whole project.

sections.topic_sentence: The two dimensions produce different profiles even within one organization or artifact.

points.text: The two dimensions produce different profiles within one system; these are not maturity levels toward the upper right.
The pattern is economic, not categorical: longevity and consequence justify investment, and mixed domains divide by surface.
Do not govern work whose reasoning will not recur and whose consequence does not justify it; use the cheapest adequate mechanism.

sections.topic_sentence: MAGE becomes a bad bargain in two broad ways.

points.text: An investment fails two ways: the asset never earns a return, or the property cannot be governed adequately.
Most systems mix surfaces; the question is which properties deserve durable representation or enforcement, not whether a project uses MAGE.

sections.topic_sentence: The evidence behind this theory comes from software engineering.

preamble_points.text: MAGE has scope conditions because it imposes costs, justified only where the structure buys something back.
The right unit of analysis is an obligation or engineering surface, not an industry label; MAGE applies unevenly within one repository.

sections.topic_sentence: The simple models above deliberately leave their parameters unspecified.

points.text: The models leave their parameters abstract; a research program can ask what determines them.
Parameterize per-attempt success and cost over task, model, representation, and harness for a fixed environment.
Cost need not mean inference alone; it can include compute, latency, tools, realization, validation, and intervention.
For sustained work the environment becomes a state variable; the research problem is identifying how much path dependence matters.
Alignment adds an escape probability q — zero for a sound gate over a decidable obligation, weaker otherwise.

sections.topic_sentence: The question is not whether agents have one fixed reliability or cost.

points.text: The empirical question is how success, cost, and escape vary across task, capability, representation, harness, and enforcement, and interact.
Modeling and Alignment can produce similar observed quality gains through different mechanisms, so experiments must separate them.

The encode-interpret-realize factorization tells a study what to measure inside p: a factorial design crossing representation quality, reasoner capability, realization task, and Alignment mechanism can estimate the stage probabilities separately.
The objective is a map of when capability, representation, iteration, and enforcement substitute or complement, not one coefficient.
Crossed experiments varying model and environment can separate capability effects, representation leverage, retry economics, and assurance.
These experiments measure representation's value to realization; it may still matter for engineering control even when capability grows.

sections.topic_sentence: These quantities suggest a further implication for automated software engineering.

points.text: Model routing treats the task as given; representation precedes model selection, so software engineering can change the problem presented to the model.
Engineering changes both the difficulty presented to the reasoner and the assurance required, as migration and authentication differ.
Representation, context, iteration, and Alignment are all realization-strategy components; the model is only one.
An automated system could jointly select model, representation, harness, enforcement, and retry budget under a task assurance bound.
The assurance bound is task-specific: routing should reflect the obligations and consequences, not just apparent difficulty.
Engineering routing asks which engineered realization strategy should receive a task, not merely which reasoner.
Task difficulty is not fixed; engineering can change it, so the optimum depends on task, capability, environment, assurance, and recurrence.
The research question becomes how cheaply a task can be engineered to be safe to delegate, not merely how difficult it is.

sections.topic_sentence: Chapter 2 offered six useful classes of engineering model, not a proof that those classes are necessary, sufficient, or minimal.

points.text: Chapter 2's six model classes were not proven necessary or minimal; representation selection is itself a research problem.
A sufficient family answers the declared questions; a minimal-useful family drops representations whose benefit fails to justify carrying cost.
A dependency graph earns its cost by answering the question and enabling a validator; a second redundant representation adds cost without leverage.
Induction recovers latent structure the system already embodies; it is not yet innovation in the strongest sense.
The stronger question is whether a reasoner can innovate representations that make relationships tractable when neither supplied nor latent.
A learning formulation asks which representation preserves the distinctions engineering questions need while suppressing irrelevant state.
An experiment compares authored, induced, and innovated representations on reasoning success, correspondence, carrying cost, and later benefit.

sections.topic_sentence: A factorial design can cleanly separate Modeling from Alignment.

points.text: Holding the gate fixed while hiding or exposing the representation separates Alignment's independence from Modeling's leverage.

sections.topic_sentence: This design should vary or observe engineered-environment quality while tracking durable throughput, defect escape, and human-attention burden over weeks or months.

points.text: A crossed longitudinal design tests whether environment quality substitutes for, complements, or barely affects model capability.
Measuring where human work goes distinguishes the narrow coding-productivity account from MAGE's broader shift of realization work.

sections.topic_sentence: Compare engineering surfaces that differ in representation and governance while holding as much surrounding repository context constant as possible.

points.text: A subsystem design with stepped introduction tests whether leverage, determinization, and assurance appear where the theory predicts.

sections.topic_sentence: Follow one failure class through its whole life: first occurrence, repeat exposure, structural recognition, local repair, any durable conversion, propagation to later work, later recurrence, and eventual maintenance or retirement of the resulting asset.

points.text: An event-centered design follows one failure class end to end, separating 'the engineer improved' from 'the environment learned.'

sections.topic_sentence: All three designs require credible measures of durable throughput, human-attention burden, environment quality, and engineering-capital return.

points.text: The designs need credible outcome measures; until then support ratio and counts stay descriptive, not proxies for value.
Commodity intelligence may make these experiments tractable by holding engine, repository, and task fixed while one factor varies.
The theory's mechanisms are not code-specific and may generalize to other engineering and knowledge work; testing that is future work.

preamble_points.text: This section turns the remaining uncertainty into a research program: what to measure and which comparisons distinguish the mechanisms.
The equations state relationships to be measured, not fixed laws.
The nine hypotheses do not require nine studies; three designs cover much of the program.

sections.topic_sentence: A reasonable objection begins with a fact: **software engineers do not spend most of their workweek typing code.** This result predates generative AI.
The first generation of agentic software-engineering research inherited the engineering object already in front of it: a repository and a software-development task.

points.text: The first agentic-SE research inherited the engineering object in front of it — a repository and a task — and asked how to make a stronger reasoner perform it.
RepoCoder, SWE-agent, and AutoCodeRover differ, but they share an orientation: improve the machinery an agent uses to act on the software artifact.
MAGE accepts that machinery and enlarges the engineering object: what durable environment should be engineered around autonomous implementation.
Retrieval, code search, interfaces, tests, and tools belong inside a governed engineering environment — pieces of a larger engineered substrate, not accessories to a coding agent.

sections.heading_text: The Old Dream, with a New Substrate
sections.topic_sentence: The ambition is older than the present substrate.

points.text: The intelligent-programming-partner dream is decades old; commodity intelligence finally lets us run much of it at production scale, where its next-order problems become visible.

sections.topic_sentence: As implementation becomes cheaper, engineers can spend more of their effort on the representations through which humans and machines reason about the system.

points.text: Retrieval asks which existing information to place before a reasoner; representation engineering asks whether the question should be expressed in a different form — only the latter changes the object of subsequent reasoning.

sections.topic_sentence: **Delegation expands; responsibility remains.** The fleet can assume work across more of the engineering lifecycle; engineers must retain sufficient control to remain responsible for intent, abstraction, evidence, tradeoffs, and acceptance.
Code review does not disappear when agents produce the code.
Chapter 5 distinguished two places engineering attention can go as realization becomes abundant.

points.text: Chapter 5 distinguished two places engineering attention can go as realization becomes abundant: operating agentic machinery, and engineering the production system around it so selected knowledge, evidence, and controls persist across acts of realization.

The distinction matters professionally because both futures can contain capable agents and very little human implementation; they differ in where scarce engineering judgment goes, and MAGE predicts increasing value in the second kind of work.

This is not a new lifecycle phase: requirements, design, validation, operation, and maintenance remain, but engineers increasingly exercise those responsibilities through the production system in which agents work.

sections.heading_text: The Disciplines That Got There First
sections.topic_sentence: Older engineering disciplines had stronger reasons to separate representation from realization.
The Siemens reconstruction illustrates what this looks like in a model-first engineering culture.

sections.heading_text: Why Software Came Late to Model-First Engineering
sections.topic_sentence: Software's economics differed from those of older engineering disciplines.
Models are the building blocks of engineering.[note: Here I mean model in the broad sense developed in Chapter 2: a purposeful reduction that preserves distinctions needed for some question.

points.text: Code is unusually expressive, precise, executable, and cheap to change, so implementation itself could carry much of the design; but the same malleability lets architecture, intent, constraints, and operational knowledge stay implicit in an artifact whose structure is continually changing.
Requirements engineering, architecture, type systems and IRs, formal methods, and model-driven approaches all share one move — represent the property at a level where it can be reasoned about.

When implementation was expensive, another representation had to justify its synchronization cost; when implementation is cheap and agents can construct, reconcile, query, and maintain representations, moving engineering knowledge out of the implementation becomes economical.

Implementation remains an important source of truth and not every representation need become authoritative; the point is that code need no longer simultaneously be the realization, the repository of system knowledge, and the surface over which reasoning occurs.

sections.topic_sentence: Software models have always faced an economic test: the reasoning or assurance they provide must repay the cost of constructing and maintaining them.
The components of MAGE have deep precedents: models, constraints, verification, external memory, structured reasoning, and autonomous software agents.

points.text: The components of MAGE have deep precedents; its claim concerns their architectural and disciplinary composition — redesign the environment when autonomous implementation becomes a primary productive substrate.

sections.topic_sentence: The first requirement is representability.
Conventional engineering is the nearest transfer because the shape of the outcome changes least.
Other engineering disciplines are therefore the easiest place to see the transfer: the outcome is often still an artifact, and much of the representational machinery already exists.

points.text: One industrial case is an instance rather than a prospect: an automotive company's agents do engineering knowledge work and no software realization, domain teams author each agent as two text files, and admission runs per tool call instead of per change.
Accounting's environment is already engineered: double-entry is an old enforcement mechanism, and the profession's controls give obligations independent paths to consequence.
Legal analysis has abundant representations, but its consequential judgments are semantic and contested — representation does not imply determinization.
The unit of transfer is the surface, not the profession — the pair shows the frontier's position is a property of the domain's obligations.

sections.topic_sentence: Scientific work is worth examining because it tests the theory rather than flattering it.

points.text: Science is the deliberately hard case: inquiry's conduct is governable, its conclusions are not.

sections.topic_sentence: The transfer conditions predict their own failures, and the failures deserve naming rather than a passing caveat.

points.text: The transfer conditions predict their own failures; the traits deserve naming rather than a caveat.

sections.topic_sentence: The broader interpretation produces a testable prediction.

preamble_points.text: Zenseact's platform fell outside this book's definition of an agentic software factory and still presented the same engineering problem, so the boundary of the software factory is not the boundary of the underlying problem.

sections.topic_sentence: MAGE increases both the leverage of engineering knowledge and the consequences of getting it wrong.

points.text: An agent can carry the method's repertoire; the engineer is distinguished by judging where the moves apply.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineering authority extends beyond technical capability.

points.text: Engineering authority follows competence and responsibility; an AI produces artifacts but cannot assume professional responsibility.
Professional licensure and responsible charge make engineering answerability institutionally explicit.
Being able to understand and challenge agentic decisions is part of the basis on which engineering authority is legitimately exercised.
Withholding authority from a system that cannot be meaningfully overseen is itself a legitimate engineering outcome.

sections.topic_sentence: One social purpose of the engineer is to be entrusted with, and answerable for, technical work too complex or consequential for ordinary individuals to undertake for themselves.[cite: bugliarello-social-function] A small bridge across the ditch in my parents' yard allowed the neighborhood kids to visit more easily, but a few boards crossing a span of three feet did not call for a structural engineer.

points.text: One social purpose of the engineer is answerability for work too consequential for ordinary individuals; GenAI can push that boundary down.
Technical capability is not social authority: the frontier is what society will let machines judge on our behalf.
Engineering capacity existing only through machine intelligence becomes critical infrastructure with no independent fallback.
Resilience also favors diversity in where machine intelligence resides; local models can be independent reserve capacity.
Implementation becoming fungible does not mean a resilient society should let independent human engineering capacity disappear.
Working with agents moves the engineer's leverage upstream, from supervising actions toward authoring and judging the environment.
Building DocAble was not deskilling: expertise moved from realizing implementation decisions to deciding what to represent, constrain, measure, and preserve.
An authored environment carries an engineer's reasoning into later work, accumulating engineering capital with unusual leverage.
Inheritance is not abdication: expert work moves to creating, evaluating, and revising the durable structure.
How the authorship responsibilities are allocated across roles should be explicit and governed.
Natural language may be one interface to the work; it is not the engineering method.

sections.heading_text: Sign-Off Moves Toward Models and Evidence
sections.topic_sentence: Imagine an agentic system in which the fleet constructs most of the implementation, maintains selected engineering representations, runs validators, and assembles evidence for the claims the design is supposed to satisfy.

points.text: Under agentic implementation, human review becomes technical acceptance of representations and evidence rather than authorship.
At scale, implementation-level inspection cannot remain the primary human assurance mechanism.
Models provide intermediate review surfaces and evidence supports their claims; neither is sufficient alone.
Models state claims, evidence justifies them, governance sets required evidence and authority, and the engineer stays answerable.
The object of review moves to models and evidence; accountability does not move.
Early evidence describes supervisory engineering work; MAGE would give that supervision better reasoning surfaces.
Real answerability requires competence and a path to change the environment, or responsibility becomes nominal.
Models remain objects of engineering: their fidelity to the system must be maintained and evidenced, not assumed.

Realization runs through an encode/interpret/realize chain; better agents improve the downstream factors but cannot recover consequential intent that was never encoded, so the residual uncertainty moves upstream.

The interpretation term is not constant across the work: for an ordinary database interaction, a familiar algorithm, or a conventional pattern, a capable agent's prior supplies much of what was left unsaid — enormously useful for exploration and prototyping.

Production raises a different question: a familiar pattern can make the agent likely to do the right thing without making the right thing explicit enough to check, so familiarity can reduce the specification needed to produce software without reducing the specification needed to assure it.

Cheapening realization moved the bottleneck rather than removing it: one expensive part of engineering became dramatically cheaper, and the opportunity now is to represent consequential requirements well enough that the new realization capacity can be used.

The engineering response is a better representation of consequential intent, not a more complete specification of the implementation: capable agents can hold realization choices open, so the engineer must represent what matters well enough to survive that freedom.

sections.topic_sentence: Software has used full-stack engineer to describe someone able to work across multiple implementation layers: interface, application logic, data, infrastructure, and deployment.

points.text: Commodity intelligence can make full-stack breadth across implementation layers easier to obtain.
MAGE requires reasoning across the full system and its lifecycle, not merely the implementation stack.
Building DocAble required breadth across many interacting domains; no single concern defined the system.
Cheap realization compresses the modeling cycle, so realization and connection amplification develop engineering judgment rather than deskilling the engineer.
Consequential judgment often requires following a property across the whole lifecycle, not just implementation.
The professional trajectory runs from full-stack toward full-system engineering, the scarcer competence.

sections.topic_sentence: If engineers increasingly review systems through representations and evidence rather than reconstructing every property from implementation, education should shift accordingly.

points.text: If review shifts to representations and evidence, education should shift accordingly.

sections.heading_text: Is there software engineering knowledge you cannot just figure out for yourself?
sections.topic_sentence: The question for software engineering education is whether there is important software engineering knowledge that practitioners cannot reasonably be expected to figure out for themselves, or whether software engineering is distinct among the engineering disciplines in being predicated on adaptability more than specific expertise.

points.text: Perhaps software engineering is adaptability, not durable technical knowledge.
Mature engineering disciplines accumulate knowledge practitioners cannot rediscover alone.
Much software-engineering wisdom is learnable through experience alone.
Many successful professionals learned software outside formal education.

sections.heading_text: What shouldn't software engineers have to figure out for themselves?
sections.topic_sentence: I would concede some of this ground.

points.text: The Alignment Principle's basic intuition is discoverable through practice.
The concession does not extend to computing's accumulated foundations.
Expertise means understanding abstractions, their guarantees, and their limits.
MAGE rests on these foundations rather than replacing them.
Delegating realization makes the technical foundations more consequential.
The curriculum remains substantially recognizable.
What changes is the allocation of attention.

sections.topic_sentence: Less educational effort may need to go toward producing routine implementation by hand, and more toward selecting abstractions, specifying properties, measuring systems, validating claims, reasoning about quality attributes, and governing autonomous work.

points.text: Shift educational emphasis toward abstractions, specification, validation, modeling, and formal methods.
Coordination becomes a technical concern at individual scale under agentic implementation capacity.

sections.topic_sentence: A capstone should therefore demonstrate more than a working artifact.

points.text: A capstone should carry the engineering case, not only a working artifact.
Program objectives change little; how students practice and demonstrate the capabilities changes.
Teach the durable principles beneath the fast-changing agent interface, not the interface itself.

sections.topic_sentence: The traditional path into software engineering runs through implementation.

points.text: GenAI erodes the implementation apprenticeship through which the profession trained senior engineers.
The entry-rung problem: how to acquire engineering judgment when routine implementation is abundant.
The profession reorganizes around responsibility for the engineered whole, not the residual machine-poor tasks.

preamble_points.text: The engineer's work is retaining informed control and responsibility for what the system should mean, not the tasks machines do poorly.

sections.topic_sentence: In the Preface, we asked:
MAGE makes three engineering moves.
Commodity intelligence changes the economics of engineering by making realization dramatically cheaper.

sections.heading_text: How much specification, and of what kind?
sections.topic_sentence: This leaves two related questions open: how much consequential intent must engineers make explicit, and in what form?

points.text: Two questions stay open — how much consequential intent must be explicit, and in what representation; the answers differ for realization and for assurance.
Capable agents already carry familiar work on sparse instruction; novelty pushes more intent back into explicit form, and future agents may infer far more.
The open question is not how much specification can disappear but what should remain explicit, in what representation, and for what purpose.
Cheap intelligence is an opportunity to build and operate engineering machinery richer than humans could economically sustain alone.
The book's last word: commodity intelligence has not come to abolish engineering, but to demand it.
